title: Reading: Plato, Apology 17a–18a
subtitle: The opening of Socrates's defense — subjunctives, optatives, and the real voice of Plato.
objectives: Read, parse, and translate the opening of Plato's Apology.
Recognize and apply all the grammar learned in Stage 4: subjunctive, optative, imperative, infinitive, conditions, indirect statement, perfect.
Understand the rhetorical style of Plato.
Build confidence for reading sustained Platonic dialogue.

sections.heading: The opening of the Apology
sections.body:
Plato's Apology is Socrates's defense speech at his trial in 399 BCE. The opening lines are among the most famous in Greek literature. Socrates begins by addressing the jury and disclaiming any skill in rhetoric.

This is unadapted Plato. The syntax is more complex than Xenophon: longer sentences, more subordination, more optatives and subjunctives. But the vocabulary is accessible, and the grammar is everything you have learned. Read it aloud first, several times. Let the rhythm of Socrates's voice carry you.

sections.heading: Apology 17a-b (excerpt)
sections.body:
Ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πεπόνθατε ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων, οὐκ οἶδα· ἐγὼ δ' οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπ' αὐτῶν ὀλίγου ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπελαθόμην, οὕτω πιθανῶς ἔλεγον. καίτοι ἀληθές γε ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν οὐδὲν εἰρήκασιν. μάλιστα δὲ αὐτῶν ἓν ἐθαύμασα τῶν πολλῶν ὧν ἐψεύσαντο, τοῦτο ἐν ᾧ ἔλεγον ὡς χρῆν ὑμᾶς εὐλαβεῖσθαι μὴ ὑπ' ἐμοῦ ἐξαπατηθῆτε ὡς δεινοῦ ὄντος λέγειν.

Gloss (abridged):
ὅτι μέν... οὐκ οἶδα — 'What... I do not know'
πεπόνθατε — you have experienced (perf. of πάσχω)
ὑπό + gen. — by
τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων — my accusers
ἐγὼ δ' οὖν — but I indeed
καὶ αὐτός — I myself also
ὀλίγου — almost
ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπελαθόμην — I forgot myself (aor. of ἐπιλανθάνομαι + gen.)
οὕτω πιθανῶς — so persuasively
ἔλεγον — they spoke (imperf.)
καίτοι — and yet
ἀληθές γε — true indeed
ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν — so to speak (idiom)
οὐδέν — nothing (acc.)
εἰρήκασιν — they have said (perf. of λέγω)
μάλιστα δέ — but especially
ἓν ἐθαύμασα — I marveled at one thing (aor.)
τῶν πολλῶν ὧν ἐψεύσαντο — of the many things which they lied about
τοῦτο ἐν ᾧ — this in which
ἔλεγον — they said
ὡς χρῆν — that it was necessary (imperf. of χρή + inf.)
ὑμᾶς εὐλαβεῖσθαι — for you to beware (pres. inf. mid. of εὐλαβέομαι)
μή... ἐξαπατηθῆτε — lest you be deceived (aor. pass. subj. of ἐξαπατάω)
ὑπ' ἐμοῦ — by me
δεινοῦ ὄντος λέγειν — (me) being clever at speaking (gen. abs.)

Translation:
What you, men of Athens, have experienced at the hands of my accusers, I do not know. But I myself, under their influence, almost forgot who I was, so persuasively did they speak. And yet, to tell the truth, they have said nothing true. But I marveled most at one of the many lies they told, the one in which they said that you should beware lest you be deceived by me, since I am a clever speaker.

sections.heading: What you have done
sections.body:
You have read the opening of Plato's Apology. You have seen subjunctives (ἐξαπατηθῆτε), optatives (if any appear later in the passage), infinitives (εὐλαβεῖσθαι, λέγειν, εἰπεῖν), perfect forms (πεπόνθατε, εἰρήκασιν), genitive absolutes (δεινοῦ ὄντος λέγειν), and indirect statement (ὡς χρῆν + infinitive). You recognized it all.

This is the threshold of advanced reading. You can now read any Greek prose with a lexicon and a commentary. The rest is vocabulary, idiom, and practice.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Answer these questions without looking back.

items.prompt: What does Socrates say he almost forgot?
Why did he almost forget himself?
items.answer: Because his accusers spoke so persuasively.

items.prompt: What does Socrates say about the truth of his accusers' statements?
What lie did Socrates marvel at most?
items.answer: The lie that the jury should beware lest they be deceived by him as a clever speaker.

items.prompt: What is the mood of ἐξαπατηθῆτε?
items.answer: Subjunctive (μή + aor. subj. = prohibition or fear).

items.prompt: What is the tense of πεπόνθατε?

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 4.12 is the final reading of Stage 4: Lysias 1, On the Murder of Eratosthenes, sections 1-10. This is conversational Attic prose, the everyday rhythm of the spoken language. After this lesson you will have read Xenophon, Plato, Lysias, and the New Testament. Stage 4 is complete.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can read the passage aloud with accurate pronunciation and can translate at least 80% of it without consulting the gloss.
